title: Integumentary System
subject: Anatomy & Physiology
description: Skin layers, glands, hair and nails, pigmentation, vitamin D, and how burns are classified.

questions.q: The largest organ of the human body is the:
questions.explain: The skin covers about 2 square meters in an adult and weighs more than any other single organ.

questions.q: Most cells of the epidermis are keratinocytes, whose main job is to produce:
questions.explain: Keratinocytes make keratin, which gives the epidermis its strength and water resistance.

questions.q: The pigment that gives skin most of its color and protects against ultraviolet radiation is:
questions.explain: Melanocytes in the epidermis produce melanin, and more melanin means darker, more UV-protected skin.

questions.q: Sunlight on the skin triggers production of which vitamin?
questions.explain: Ultraviolet light converts a cholesterol-based molecule in the skin into vitamin D, which is needed for calcium absorption.

questions.q: The dermis is the skin layer that contains:
options: Blood vessels, nerves, glands, and hair follicles
questions.explain: The living dermis holds the skin's vessels, sensory receptors, sweat and oil glands, and follicles; the fat layer below it is the hypodermis.

questions.q: The apocrine sweat glands, which become active at puberty, are concentrated in the:
questions.explain: Apocrine glands in the armpits and groin release a thicker sweat that bacteria break down into body odor.

questions.q: The tiny muscle that contracts in cold or fear to make a hair stand upright is the:
questions.explain: Contraction of the arrector pili produces goosebumps and helps trap a layer of warm air in furry animals.

questions.q: A burn that destroys both the epidermis and the full dermis, leaving the area white or charred and often painless, is classified as a:
questions.explain: Full-thickness burns destroy nerve endings, which is why they may not hurt, and they usually require skin grafts.

questions.q: Sebaceous glands keep hair and skin soft by secreting an oil called:
questions.explain: Sebum lubricates the skin and hair and has mild antibacterial action; blocked sebaceous glands contribute to acne.

questions.q: Fingernails and toenails grow from dividing cells in the:
questions.explain: The nail matrix at the base of the nail produces new keratin cells that push the nail plate forward.

rounds.title: Integumentary System
rounds.desc: Skin layers, glands, hair and nails, pigmentation, vitamin D, and how burns are classified.

title: Skeletal System
subject: Anatomy & Physiology
description: Bones, joints, and how the skeleton supports, protects, and renews the body.

questions.q: How many bones are in the typical adult human skeleton?
questions.explain: Adults have 206 bones. Babies are born with about 300, but many fuse together as the skeleton develops, which is why the adult number is smaller.

questions.q: Which bone is the longest and strongest in the human body?
questions.explain: The femur (thigh bone) is the longest and strongest bone, supporting the body's weight during walking and running. It can bear up to 30 times an adult's body weight.

questions.q: The shoulder joint is classified as which type of joint?
questions.explain: The shoulder is a ball-and-socket synovial joint, which gives it the widest range of motion of any joint — at the cost of stability, which is why shoulder dislocations are common.

questions.q: Which cells are responsible for breaking down and resorbing bone tissue?
questions.explain: Osteoclasts dissolve bone matrix during remodeling. Osteoblasts do the opposite — they build new bone — while osteocytes are mature bone cells that maintain the matrix.

questions.q: Which bones make up the axial skeleton?
options: Skull, vertebral column, and rib cage
questions.explain: The axial skeleton forms the body's central axis: the skull, vertebral column, sternum, and ribs (80 bones). Everything else — limbs and girdles — belongs to the appendicular skeleton.

questions.q: Which structure connects a muscle to a bone?
questions.explain: Tendons anchor muscle to bone so contraction can move the skeleton. Ligaments do a different job: they connect bone to bone across a joint.

questions.q: Fontanelles — the soft spots a baby is born with — are found in which bones?
questions.explain: Fontanelles are gaps between the flat bones of an infant's skull. They let the skull flex during birth and expand as the brain grows, then close by about 18 months of age.

questions.q: What is the primary function of red bone marrow?
questions.explain: Red marrow performs hematopoiesis — it produces red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Yellow marrow, by contrast, mostly stores fat.

questions.q: The seven vertebrae located in the neck are called the:
questions.explain: The spine has 7 cervical (neck), 12 thoracic (mid-back), and 5 lumbar (lower back) vertebrae. The first two cervical vertebrae — the atlas and axis — allow nodding and head rotation.

questions.q: The patella (kneecap) is best classified as which type of bone?
questions.explain: The patella is a sesamoid bone — one embedded within a tendon (here, the quadriceps tendon). Sesamoid bones protect tendons and improve a muscle's leverage.

title: Muscular System
subject: Anatomy & Physiology
description: Muscle types, contraction mechanics, and the muscles that move the body.

questions.q: Which muscle is the prime mover for flexing the forearm at the elbow?
questions.explain: The biceps brachii is the main elbow flexor. The triceps brachii works as its antagonist, extending the forearm — most limb movements are produced by such opposing pairs.

questions.q: Cardiac muscle tissue is best described as:
options: Smooth and found in the heart wall only when diseased
questions.explain: Cardiac muscle is striated like skeletal muscle but involuntary, and its cells are linked by intercalated discs that let the heart contract as one coordinated unit.

questions.q: The smallest functional unit of a muscle fiber — the unit that actually contracts — is the:
questions.explain: The sarcomere, spanning from one Z disc to the next, is where actin and myosin filaments slide past each other to shorten the muscle. A motor unit is a neuron plus all the fibers it controls — a larger structure.

questions.q: During muscle contraction, calcium ions bind to which protein to expose actin's binding sites?
questions.explain: Calcium released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds troponin, which shifts tropomyosin off actin's myosin-binding sites. Without that calcium signal, contraction cannot begin.

questions.q: The diaphragm is the primary muscle of:
questions.explain: When the diaphragm contracts it flattens and drops, expanding the chest cavity and drawing air in. It performs roughly 75% of the work of quiet breathing.

questions.q: Slow-twitch (Type I) muscle fibers are best suited for:
questions.explain: Type I fibers are packed with mitochondria and myoglobin, resist fatigue, and rely on aerobic metabolism — built for endurance. Fast-twitch fibers generate power but tire quickly.

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter is released at the neuromuscular junction to trigger contraction?
questions.explain: Motor neurons release acetylcholine (ACh) onto the muscle fiber's motor end plate, opening ion channels that start an action potential. Botulinum toxin causes paralysis by blocking ACh release.

questions.q: The triceps brachii is the antagonist of which muscle?
questions.explain: An antagonists oppose each other's actions: the biceps flexes the elbow while the triceps extends it. When one contracts, the other must relax for smooth movement.

questions.q: Rigor mortis (stiffening after death) occurs because:
options: Calcium floods the muscles and locks them contracted
No new ATP is made, so myosin heads cannot detach from actin
Lactic acid permanently hardens the fibers
Blood clots form inside the muscle tissue
questions.explain: Detaching myosin from actin requires ATP. After death, ATP production stops, so cross-bridges stay locked and muscles stiffen until tissues begin to break down.

questions.q: Which is the largest muscle in the human body?
questions.explain: The gluteus maximus is the largest muscle by volume. It keeps the trunk upright and powers hip extension in climbing, running, and rising from a chair.

title: Cardiovascular System
subject: Anatomy & Physiology
description: The heart, blood vessels, and how blood circulates through the body.

questions.q: Which chamber of the heart pumps oxygenated blood out to the systemic circulation?
questions.explain: The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it must generate enough pressure to drive blood through the entire body via the aorta. The right ventricle only pumps to the nearby lungs.

questions.q: The natural pacemaker of the heart is the:
questions.explain: The SA node fires fastest (~60-100 times/min) and sets the heart's rhythm. If it fails, the AV node and other tissues can take over at slower backup rates.

questions.q: Which valve prevents blood from flowing backward from the left ventricle into the left atrium?
questions.explain: The mitral valve sits between the left atrium and left ventricle and snaps shut during ventricular contraction. A leaking mitral valve causes a characteristic murmur.

questions.q: In the cardiac cycle, systole refers to:
questions.explain: Systole is the contraction phase (ventricles squeezing blood out), and diastole is the relaxation/filling phase. Blood pressure readings are written as systolic over diastolic.

questions.q: Oxygen-poor blood from the body returns to the heart through the:
questions.explain: The superior and inferior venae cavae dump systemic venous blood into the right atrium. Note the exception: pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood (from the lungs) to the left atrium.

questions.q: When taking a manual blood pressure, the stethoscope is placed over which artery?
questions.explain: The cuff is wrapped around the upper arm and Korotkoff sounds are heard over the brachial artery. The radial pulse is for heart-rate counting, not blood pressure.

questions.q: The very first branches to come off the aorta supply the heart itself and are called the:
questions.explain: The coronary arteries branch from the aortic root and feed the heart muscle. A blockage here causes a myocardial infarction — a heart attack.

questions.q: The normal resting heart rate range for a healthy adult is:
questions.explain: 60-100 bpm is the normal resting range. Below 60 is bradycardia and above 100 is tachycardia — though trained athletes often rest below 60 and remain healthy.

questions.q: Which type of blood vessel contains one-way valves that help prevent backflow?
questions.explain: Veins are low-pressure vessels, so valves — especially in the limbs — keep blood moving toward the heart against gravity. Arteries don't need valves because ventricular pressure keeps flow one-way.

questions.q: The muscular walls of the heart receive their own oxygenated blood supply from the:
questions.explain: Despite being full of blood, the heart's thick walls cannot absorb enough oxygen from chamber blood — the coronary circulation exists specifically to feed the myocardium.

title: Nervous System
subject: Anatomy & Physiology
description: Neurons, the brain, the spinal cord, and how signals travel through the body.

questions.q: The basic structural and functional unit of the nervous system is the:
questions.explain: The neuron generates and transmits electrical signals. Glial cells support neurons but don't conduct impulses themselves — neurons are the signaling cells.

questions.q: Which part of a neuron receives incoming signals from other neurons?
questions.explain: Dendrites are the branched receivers that collect synaptic input and funnel it toward the cell body. Axons carry the outgoing signal away to the next cell.

questions.q: In the central nervous system, myelin is produced by:
questions.explain: Oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons; Schwann cells do the same job in the peripheral nervous system. Multiple sclerosis is the autoimmune destruction of CNS myelin.

questions.q: The division of the autonomic nervous system responsible for fight-or-flight responses is the:
questions.explain: The sympathetic division raises heart rate, dilates airways, and mobilizes energy for action. The parasympathetic division handles rest-and-digest functions like slowing the heart and stimulating digestion.

questions.q: Which brain structure is most responsible for balance and coordination of movement?
questions.explain: The cerebellum fine-tunes movement, balance, and posture. Damage causes ataxia — clumsy, uncoordinated movements — while the cerebrum handles conscious thought.

questions.q: The spinal cord typically ends at the level of which vertebrae?
questions.explain: The cord tapers into the conus medullaris around L1-L2 in adults. That's why lumbar punctures are done lower, at L3-L4 — to sample CSF without stabbing the cord.

questions.q: A typical resting membrane potential of a neuron is approximately:
questions.explain: The inside of a resting neuron sits about -70 mV relative to the outside, maintained by the sodium-potassium pump and potassium leak channels. An action potential briefly reverses this to about +30 mV.

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter is most closely associated with reward, motivation, and Parkinson's disease?
questions.explain: Dopamine drives reward and movement initiation. Parkinson's results from the loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra, causing tremor and rigidity.

questions.q: The corpus callosum connects the:
questions.explain: The corpus callosum is the great band of fibers letting the left and right hemispheres communicate. Cutting it (a rare epilepsy treatment) creates 'split-brain' patients.

questions.q: A simple reflex arc follows which pathway?
options: Receptor, sensory neuron, interneuron, motor neuron, effector
Receptor, motor neuron, sensory neuron, effector
Sensory neuron, receptor, motor neuron, effector
Receptor, interneuron, sensory neuron, motor neuron, effector
questions.explain: Sensory input travels from the receptor through a sensory neuron to the spinal cord, gets processed (often by an interneuron), and exits via a motor neuron to the effector — all without waiting for the brain.

title: Endocrine System
subject: Anatomy & Physiology
description: The major glands and hormones: pituitary, thyroid, adrenals, pancreas, and how negative feedback keeps hormone levels in range.

questions.q: The gland often called the master gland because it controls several other endocrine glands is the:
questions.explain: The pituitary, directed by the hypothalamus, releases hormones that drive the thyroid, adrenals, and gonads.

questions.q: Which hormone lowers blood glucose by helping cells take glucose in?
questions.explain: Beta cells of the pancreas release insulin after meals, moving glucose out of the blood and into cells.

questions.q: Thyroid hormones T3 and T4 primarily regulate the body's:
questions.explain: Thyroid hormone sets how fast cells burn energy, affecting body temperature, heart rate, and weight.

questions.q: The adrenal medulla releases epinephrine (adrenaline) mainly in response to:
options: Acute stress, as part of the fight-or-flight response
questions.explain: Epinephrine raises heart rate, blood pressure, and blood glucose to prepare the body for action.

questions.q: The anterior pituitary hormone that stimulates milk production after childbirth is:
questions.explain: Prolactin drives milk production in the mammary glands, while oxytocin triggers milk release.

questions.q: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) acts to:
questions.explain: PTH raises blood calcium by drawing calcium from bone, increasing absorption in the gut, and conserving it in the kidneys.

questions.q: Melatonin, which helps set the sleep-wake cycle, is secreted by the:
questions.explain: The pineal gland releases melatonin in response to darkness, helping regulate circadian rhythm.

questions.q: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH, also called vasopressin) causes the kidneys to:
options: Reabsorb more water, producing more concentrated urine
questions.explain: ADH inserts water channels in the collecting ducts, conserving body water when you are dehydrated.

questions.q: Glucagon, the hormone that raises blood glucose by releasing stored glucose from the liver, is made by:
questions.explain: Alpha cells secrete glucagon between meals to keep blood glucose from falling too low.

questions.q: Diabetes insipidus, which causes very large volumes of dilute urine, results from a deficiency of:
questions.explain: Without enough ADH the kidneys cannot conserve water. Despite the shared name, it is unrelated to the blood-sugar problem in diabetes mellitus.
